title: MTRX™ Field Series No. 03 · Cons and cults · Kevin Cecil

cards.name: Why this course exists
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why this course exists" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Curiosity first: every stop answers a real question, and every answer has a source.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The question bank and the map
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The question bank and the map" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: This course answers questions, not chapters. If your question is not on the list, ask it and it becomes a stop.

cards.name: Who joins, and why it is not stupidity
cards.q: What did Barker's tracking of Unification Church workshop guests mostly show?
options: Most guests walked away, so the workshops were far weaker than the brainwashing story said
Guests joined at the same rate as any church, so the group was no different at all
Most guests joined, because the workshops overrode their judgment with a hidden technique
cards.why: About 9 in 10 never joined, and most joiners left within two years. That does not make the group harmless; it makes the zombie story wrong.

cards.name: Who joins, and why it is not stupidity
cards.q: In the Lofland and Stark model, what usually opens the door into a group?
options: A hidden personality flaw that makes the recruit easy to deceive
A bond with a member, often before the doctrine makes any sense
A strong argument for the doctrine, long before any friendship forms
cards.why: Recruitment travels through relationships. Greil and Rudy found bonds and intense time together were the two conditions present in every case.

cards.name: Who joins, and why it is not stupidity
cards.q: Why does high intelligence give weak protection against joining?
options: Intelligent people are rarely approached, so they never practise saying no
It protects well, which is why groups mostly recruit people with little schooling
A sharp mind can build strong reasons for a choice that loneliness already made
cards.why: Intelligence serves whatever need is driving it. Timing, transitions and relationships predict joining better than IQ.

cards.name: Who joins, and why it is not stupidity
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Who joins, and why it is not stupidity" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Nobody joins a cult on purpose. People join friends, then a cause, and only later learn what the group was.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: What a cult is, and why the word is a fight
cards.q: Which question best separates a demanding group from a coercive one?
options: Are its beliefs unusual compared with the religions around it?
Is its founder still alive and still leading it day to day?
Can members leave without losing their money, home and family?
cards.why: Exit cost is the strongest signal. Strange beliefs and living founders are common in harmless groups.

cards.name: What a cult is, and why the word is a fight
cards.q: Why did researchers move to the term 'new religious movement'?
options: Because 'cult' had become a verdict rather than a description
Because 1970s studies had proven every new group was harmless
Because courts had banned the word 'cult' in academic papers
cards.why: The new term describes a group's position and novelty. Whether harm occurred is a separate question that needs evidence.

cards.name: What a cult is, and why the word is a fight
cards.q: In this course, what does 'high-demand group' point at?
options: How unusual the group's beliefs are compared with mainstream ones
How much the group asks for in time, money, loyalty and obedience
How many members the group recruited in its first five years
cards.why: It names demands and mechanisms, so it works for religious, political, wellness and business groups alike.

cards.name: What a cult is, and why the word is a fight
cards.q: Page closed: explain "What a cult is, and why the word is a fight" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Don't diagnose a group by its beliefs. Map who can punish whom, and what it costs to leave.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The toolkit: Lifton's eight
cards.q: Where did Lifton's eight criteria come from?
options: Interviews with people put through thought reform in 1950s China
Laboratory experiments on obedience run at Yale in the 1960s
A study of American cult members during the 1970s cult panic
cards.why: Lifton published in 1961, before the American cult scare, so the themes describe any closed ideological world.

cards.name: The toolkit: Lifton's eight
cards.q: What does Lifton mean by 'dispensing of existence'?
options: Members must hand over their possessions to the leader when they join
The leader claims the power to heal any illness through faith alone
The group decides who deserves to exist with dignity, and who does not
cards.why: Insiders are saved; outsiders and leavers are lost, ill or evil. It is what makes leaving feel like dying.

cards.name: The toolkit: Lifton's eight
cards.q: Why should you treat the BITE model with some caution?
options: It looks only at behaviour, so it misses thought and emotion entirely
It is a useful prompt, but it was never validated as a diagnostic test
It was formally rejected by the APA in the same 1987 report as Singer's
cards.why: The 1987 rejection was of Singer's task force report. BITE covers behaviour, information, thought and emotion, but lacks independent validation.

cards.name: The toolkit: Lifton's eight
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The toolkit: Lifton's eight" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: A technique is not magic. Its power comes from repetition, dependency and the cost of dissent.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Cutting the cord: why cults isolate you
cards.q: In organisational terms, why does isolation help a coercive group?
options: It keeps out journalists and spies who might expose its money
It removes rival information, emotional refuge and the road out
It saves the money members would otherwise spend on visits home
cards.why: Outside ties supply information, rest and an exit. Closing all three is the point; secrecy and money are side effects.

cards.name: Cutting the cord: why cults isolate you
cards.q: What does 'fright without solution' describe?
options: Fear that fades once a member fully accepts the group's doctrine
Fear of a danger with no fix, such as death or serious illness
Fear whose source is also the only offered source of safety
cards.why: The member runs toward the very thing frightening her, which is why fear deepens the bond instead of breaking it.

cards.name: Cutting the cord: why cults isolate you
cards.q: A friend's sister has joined an intense group. What is the best first move?
options: Keep the bridge open: stay warm, ask concrete questions, no ultimatums
Send her every critical article about the group as soon as you can
Give her a clear choice today: the group or the family, never both
cards.why: Facts arrive through a channel the group has marked hostile. A warm bridge and practical help are what leavers say mattered.

cards.name: Cutting the cord: why cults isolate you
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Cutting the cord: why cults isolate you" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The real question is not who is forbidden to leave. It is what a person would lose by leaving.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Why cults work: strictness, sacrifice and dissonance
cards.q: In Iannaccone's model, what do strict rules mainly do?
options: Frighten members so much that nobody ever dares to leave
Prove the doctrine true, since people only sacrifice for truth
Screen out free riders, so the members who stay give more
cards.why: Strictness is a filter that makes the club better for those who stay. It is silent on whether the doctrine is true.

cards.name: Why cults work: strictness, sacrifice and dissonance
cards.q: What is the fairest status of When Prophecy Fails today?
options: Influential, but a single covert case study with method problems
A hoax that its authors later admitted they had invented
A replicated lab result showing belief always grows after failure
cards.why: The general idea of escalating commitment is well supported. The famous case itself is thin evidence.

cards.name: Why cults work: strictness, sacrifice and dissonance
cards.q: Why does 'I was wrong' get harder to say the longer you stay?
options: Members slowly lose the ability to think critically at all
Each sacrifice makes leaving mean that the costs were wasted
The doctrine gets more convincing the longer it is studied
cards.why: Escalation of commitment: every public act raises the price of admitting error. Thinking still works; it gets aimed at defending the cost.

cards.name: Why cults work: strictness, sacrifice and dissonance
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why cults work: strictness, sacrifice and dissonance" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Sacrifice can signal commitment, but commitment is not evidence.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Belonging and identity: the happiest time of my life
cards.q: What did Tajfel's minimal group studies show?
options: People treat random groups fairly unless money for themselves is at stake
People favour their own group even when it rests on a trivial label
People favour only groups that share deep values and a long history
cards.why: A meaningless label, Klee or Kandinsky, was enough. Nothing was at stake for the boys personally.

cards.name: Belonging and identity: the happiest time of my life
cards.q: What does identity fusion mean?
options: The person belongs to two rival groups at the very same time
The person loses every trace of their own individual personality
The person feels the group's fate as their own personal fate
cards.why: Fused people keep a strong personal self. The border between self and group becomes porous.

cards.name: Belonging and identity: the happiest time of my life
cards.q: A former member says: 'Best years of my life, and it was abuse.' What is the best reading?
options: Both can be true: the belonging was real, the structure was coercive
She is confused, because real abuse can never feel like the best years
She is exaggerating one half to protect the story she now tells
cards.why: Belonging rewards and coercive structures coexist. Treating either half as fake misreads the experience.

cards.name: Belonging and identity: the happiest time of my life
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Belonging and identity: the happiest time of my life" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The happiest memory is evidence of belonging, not evidence that the system was safe.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Case file: Jonestown, read with everything
cards.q: Which statement about the Jonestown drink is accurate?
options: The poison was mixed into Flavor Aid, not into Kool-Aid
There was no drink at all; every death was by injection
The poison was mixed into Kool-Aid, just as the phrase says
cards.why: Kool-Aid packets were in the pantry, but Flavor Aid was used that day, according to the Jonestown archive.

cards.name: Case file: Jonestown, read with everything
cards.q: Why do many scholars prefer 'murder-suicide' for Jonestown?
options: The deaths were ordered from the US, so nobody in Guyana chose
Investigators found that nobody there drank the poison willingly
Hundreds of the dead were children, and many adults did not choose
cards.why: 304 of the dead at Jonestown were minors. Calling it suicide erases what was done to them, though some adults did choose.

cards.name: Case file: Jonestown, read with everything
cards.q: Which combination best explains why Jonestown ended in violence?
options: A closed, isolated world, a threatened leader, rehearsals and no way back
Unusual religious beliefs held by an unusually large number of members
A naturally charismatic leader combined with unusually gullible followers
cards.why: Strange beliefs and charisma are common in groups that never turn violent. The combination of conditions predicts danger.

cards.name: Case file: Jonestown, read with everything
cards.q: Drill "Read a case in six lenses": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Pick a real group from a documentary or a long article 2) Find one concrete detail for each of Stops 1.1 to 1.6 3) Mark which details are documented and which are only claimed 4) Write the one combination that made it dangerous Usual mistake: Reaching for "brainwashing" instead of naming the specific mechanism and the evidence for it.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Case file: Jonestown, read with everything
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Case file: Jonestown, read with everything" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The warning sign is not a strange belief. It is a closed world under pressure, with no dignified way out.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The leader's motive: true believer, fraud, or both
cards.q: A leader fakes miracles. What can you safely conclude?
options: That he is a pure fraud who never believed a word of his own message
Very little about his belief: faking proof and sincere faith often coexist
That he must be mentally ill, since sane believers never fake proof
cards.why: Pious fraud is old and common. Belief is a weak predictor; incentives and checks on power are stronger.

cards.name: The leader's motive: true believer, fraud, or both
cards.q: Which question best predicts whether a leader is dangerous?
options: Does the leader sincerely believe the message he preaches?
How unusual is the leader's doctrine compared with others?
What happens to a follower who refuses an order or leaves?
cards.why: If refusal is punished, sincerity is irrelevant. If refusal is safe, even an odd leader is low risk.

cards.name: The leader's motive: true believer, fraud, or both
cards.q: Why do motives tend to drift from mission toward privilege?
options: Leaders are frauds from the start and simply reveal it over the years
Obedience brings rewards and doubt threatens them, so doubt gets punished
Followers demand harsher rules as they grow more committed to the group
cards.why: Rewards accumulate whatever the leader believes, and protecting them gives him reasons to silence doubt.

cards.name: The leader's motive: true believer, fraud, or both
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The leader's motive: true believer, fraud, or both" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Don't ask whether the guru believes. Ask what happens when someone says no.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The guru pattern: Storr's Feet of Clay and the narcissism question
cards.q: In Storr's pattern, what usually comes just before a guru's revelation?
options: A crisis, such as a breakdown, an illness or an expulsion
A period of great popularity and many close friendships
Formal training in theology at a respected seminary
cards.why: Isolated youth, then crisis, then a private revelation the guru declares true for everyone.

cards.name: The guru pattern: Storr's Feet of Clay and the narcissism question
cards.q: Why does Storr say gurus need disciples rather than friends?
options: Disciples confirm the guru's sense of self; friends can disagree
Disciples pay more money, which keeps the movement funded
Friends tend to drift away, while disciples stay for life
cards.why: The guru's self-image depends on admiration, so equals who can say no are a threat.

cards.name: The guru pattern: Storr's Feet of Clay and the narcissism question
cards.q: What best explains why sexual and financial abuse recur in cults?
options: Members come from backgrounds that make abuse feel normal
Most leaders start as predators and found groups to hide it
Power that nobody can refuse or audit makes abuse cheap
cards.why: Structural impunity, not just personal appetite. The defences are audit, safeguarding and safe refusal.

cards.name: The guru pattern: Storr's Feet of Clay and the narcissism question
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The guru pattern: Storr's Feet of Clay and the narcissism question" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: A guru needs disciples, not friends. Friends can say no.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Charisma: why followers grant it
cards.q: For Weber, what makes authority charismatic?
options: A legal office that gives its holder the right to command
Followers' devotion to a person they see as extraordinary
A family line that has ruled the group for generations
cards.why: Weber's three types: traditional (custom), legal-rational (rules), charismatic (devotion to an extraordinary person).

cards.name: Charisma: why followers grant it
cards.q: Why is charismatic authority unstable?
options: It rests on written rules that members can easily challenge
It passes automatically to the eldest child of the leader
It has to keep proving itself with new signs and victories
cards.why: Without fresh proof, recognition fades. That pressure helps explain why charismatic groups escalate.

cards.name: Charisma: why followers grant it
cards.q: What did Platow and colleagues find about charisma?
options: Charismatic leaders were rated lower by their own group members
Leaders seen as typical of the group were judged more charismatic
Charisma ratings depended only on the leader's speaking skill
cards.why: Same words, different perceived typicality, different charisma. The audience supplies part of it.

cards.name: Charisma: why followers grant it
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Charisma: why followers grant it" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Charisma is not what the leader has. It is what the relationship keeps producing.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Why we need leaders at all: prestige, dominance and following
cards.q: What did van Vugt's review link most strongly with leadership?
options: Initiative, competence and generosity, rather than dominance
Physical size and aggression, as in other primate groups
Family wealth and inherited rank within the community
cards.why: Groups grant leadership to useful people. Dominance is a separate route to status.

cards.name: Why we need leaders at all: prestige, dominance and following
cards.q: How does prestige differ from dominance?
options: Prestige comes from wealth; dominance comes from age and wisdom
Prestige lasts for life; dominance vanishes after one defeat
Prestige is freely given for skill; dominance is taken by fear
cards.why: Prestige is paid in voluntary deference that followers can withdraw. Dominance punishes withdrawal.

cards.name: Why we need leaders at all: prestige, dominance and following
cards.q: What do cults typically do to the ancient follower bargain?
options: Remove the leader's special skill, so followers slowly lose interest
Remove the right to stop following, so respect becomes submission
Remove all hierarchy, so that every member takes a turn leading
cards.why: Prestige converted into dominance: switching becomes betrayal and leaving costs everything.

cards.name: Why we need leaders at all: prestige, dominance and following
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why we need leaders at all: prestige, dominance and following" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Healthy followership keeps the power to compare, switch and criticise.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Entrepreneurs of identity: how leaders build the "we"
cards.q: What do Haslam, Reicher and Platow mean by an entrepreneur of identity?
options: A leader who crafts and sells a shared sense of who 'we' are
A leader who copies the identity of a more successful group
A leader who starts a company to fund the group's activities
cards.why: Effective leaders define the group, embody it, and turn it into rituals and structures.

cards.name: Entrepreneurs of identity: how leaders build the "we"
cards.q: What turns identity leadership into something coercive?
options: A group having its own songs, symbols or history
One person claiming to be the only author of the 'we'
Any leader talking about what the group stands for
cards.why: Rituals and identity talk are normal. Exclusive ownership is what makes dissent equal betrayal.

cards.name: Entrepreneurs of identity: how leaders build the "we"
cards.q: Why are uncertain people drawn to sharp-edged groups?
options: Sharp-edged groups usually pay new members more money
They have weaker reasoning skills than people who feel certain
A clear, all-explaining identity makes the uncertainty go away
cards.why: Uncertainty about self and world raises the appeal of groups with clear lines and confident leaders.

cards.name: Entrepreneurs of identity: how leaders build the "we"
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Entrepreneurs of identity: how leaders build the "we"" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The leader who defines 'us' doesn't need to give orders.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: When the leader dies, fails or is exposed
cards.q: What did Weber call turning a leader's charisma into lasting structures?
options: Routinisation
Secularisation
Rationalisation
cards.why: Offices, scripture, rituals and succession rules let charisma outlive the person. Rationalisation is a related but broader Weber idea.

cards.name: When the leader dies, fails or is exposed
cards.q: What happened to the Unification Church after Sun Myung Moon died in 2012?
options: It passed peacefully to a council of elders chosen by members
It dissolved within a year as members returned to their families
It split into three factions, each claiming to be his true heir
cards.why: His widow and two sons each claimed succession, and the factions fought over assets in court.

cards.name: When the leader dies, fails or is exposed
cards.q: Why can the exposure of a leader briefly strengthen a group's core?
options: Exposed leaders usually confess and win back the trust of their followers
Loyalists read exposure as persecution, which confirms the group's story
Exposure brings media attention that recruits many new members at once
cards.why: Admitting deception costs identity; persecution is the cheaper story. The edges fall away while the core hardens.

cards.name: When the leader dies, fails or is exposed
cards.q: Page closed: explain "When the leader dies, fails or is exposed" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: A movement survives its founder only if it built something he cannot take with him.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Case file: NXIVM, a coaching company that branded women
cards.q: What did NXIVM's secret group DOS demand before a woman could join?
options: Collateral, such as nude photos or other compromising material
A signed statement renouncing all contact with her family
A large cash fee paid directly into the leader's bank account
cards.why: Collateral guaranteed secrecy and obedience: Lifton's confession turned into leverage.

cards.name: Case file: NXIVM, a coaching company that branded women
cards.q: Which idea from this file best explains NXIVM's rank system?
options: Prestige turned into dominance, with rank tied to recruiting
Routinisation that let the group outlive its founder
Charisma turned into a legal office that members elected
cards.why: Admiration for Raniere's supposed genius was converted, through sashes and the stripe path, into obedience.

cards.name: Case file: NXIVM, a coaching company that branded women
cards.q: What is the fairest lesson of the NXIVM case?
options: Self-improvement courses are a form of cult and are best avoided
Wealthy and famous people are especially easy to manipulate
An ordinary course structure turned coercive under one unaccountable man
cards.why: The format was ordinary. Ownership of the 'we', plus no audit, made it dangerous.

cards.name: Case file: NXIVM, a coaching company that branded women
cards.q: Drill "Read a leader through five lenses": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Pick a leader from a documentary, a news case or a film 2) Write his motive mix: mission, self, appetite 3) Look for Storr's three beats in his life story 4) Show how followers gave him charisma, and where prestige turned into dominance 5) Name who owned the we, and what happened when he fell Usual mistake: Diagnosing him (narcissist, psychopath) instead of describing what he did and what the structure let him do.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Case file: NXIVM, a coaching company that branded women
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Case file: NXIVM, a coaching company that branded women" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: NXIVM looked like a business course. The danger was never the format. It was one man who owned the 'we'.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The sociological lens: Weber, Durkheim and collective effervescence
cards.q: What does collective effervescence describe?
options: A hidden technique that leaders use to plant beliefs in a crowd
The charged feeling a group makes when it gathers and moves together
The calm that settles over members once they stop asking questions
cards.why: Durkheim meant the real energy of gathering. The feeling is genuine; the explanation a group attaches to it is a separate claim.

cards.name: The sociological lens: Weber, Durkheim and collective effervescence
cards.q: What did Durkheim's Suicide suggest about social integration?
options: Harm falls steadily as groups grow tighter, so more belonging is always safer
Harm rises at both ends: too few ties, and a group that swallows the self
Integration made no measurable difference once income was accounted for
cards.why: Egoistic suicide came with weak ties, altruistic suicide with very tight ones. Belonging protects; total belonging is its own risk.

cards.name: The sociological lens: Weber, Durkheim and collective effervescence
cards.q: In Stark and Bainbridge's terms, what makes a group a cult rather than a sect?
options: It brings a new or imported tradition, not a break from an old one
It harms its members, while a sect is a harmless religious club
It has a living leader, while a sect is run by a written rulebook
cards.why: Both live in tension with society. A sect renews an existing tradition; a cult brings a new one. No verdict on harm is built in.

cards.name: The sociological lens: Weber, Durkheim and collective effervescence
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The sociological lens: Weber, Durkheim and collective effervescence" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The high is real. The explanation the group staples onto it is the part you are allowed to check.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Recruitment runs on networks, and some cults become world religions
cards.q: What did Stark and Lofland notice about the first American converts they watched?
options: They responded to radio spots and public meetings far more than to friends
They had studied the doctrine for years before ever meeting a member
They were friends and relatives of members, not strangers moved by ads
cards.why: Radio and public meetings yielded nothing. Converts came through ties to members.

cards.name: Recruitment runs on networks, and some cults become world religions
cards.q: Why does a 40% per decade growth rate matter so much in Stark's model?
options: A small steady rate compounds into millions without any miracle
It shows growth came mostly from huge public conversion events
It proves the ancient records counted every single member exactly
cards.why: About 3.4% a year, compounded for centuries, turns 1,000 people into about 6.3 million.

cards.name: Recruitment runs on networks, and some cults become world religions
cards.q: Which statement about cults and world religions is the most careful?
options: Large faiths began as small movements in tension with their world
Every world religion began as a cult and simply grew out of it
World religions never began small; they started with state support
cards.why: Cult is a contested label. Small, high-tension movement describes the start without the slogan.

cards.name: Recruitment runs on networks, and some cults become world religions
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Recruitment runs on networks, and some cults become world religions" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Growth that looks miraculous from far away usually looks like friendship up close.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The brainwashing fight: Singer, the APA and the courts
cards.q: What did the APA board actually say about the 1987 task force report?
options: It rejected the report and said it lacked the information to take a position
It endorsed the report and asked courts to treat brainwashing as proven
It ruled that no group had ever manipulated a member in any harmful way
cards.why: Both lines matter. The report was rejected; the question was left open.

cards.name: The brainwashing fight: Singer, the APA and the courts
cards.q: What did the Fishman court decide in 1990?
options: Experts could testify, but only if they had been members themselves
Brainwashing testimony lacked general acceptance, so it was excluded
Scientology was guilty of controlling the defendant, so he went free
cards.why: The Frye test asks whether a theory is accepted in its field. The court found it was not.

cards.name: The brainwashing fight: Singer, the APA and the courts
cards.q: Which claim did California's Supreme Court allow to go forward in Molko (1988)?
options: Kidnapping, because the church had physically held the two recruits
Brainwashing, because a secret technique had erased their free will
Fraud, because recruiters allegedly hid which group was inviting them
cards.why: Deception about the group's identity was treated as ordinary fraud, not protected religion.

cards.name: The brainwashing fight: Singer, the APA and the courts
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The brainwashing fight: Singer, the APA and the courts" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Nobody proved a mind-control technique. Plenty of people proved they were lied to about what they were joining.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The cult panic: deprogrammers and what they got wrong
cards.q: What made deprogramming self-defeating as a rescue method?
options: It was too gentle, so members simply ignored the arguments offered
It relied on courts, which always sided with the groups being opposed
It used seizure, isolation and pressure, the very methods it condemned
cards.why: Abduction and confinement mirrored the control it claimed to fight, and courts treated it as crime.

cards.name: The cult panic: deprogrammers and what they got wrong
cards.q: What did the McMartin preschool case finally show?
options: A satanic network was proven in court and its leaders were imprisoned
Years of trials built on leading interviews ended with no convictions
Children never report abuse, so the case was dropped before any trial
cards.why: About $15 million, trials from 1987 to 1990, and no convictions. The interviewing method was central to the collapse.

cards.name: The cult panic: deprogrammers and what they got wrong
cards.q: What is the double lesson of the cult panic?
options: Real harms existed, and the panic still hurt innocent people
The harms were invented, so every warning about cults was false
The panic was justified, so its methods should not be criticised
cards.why: Both halves matter: a panic distorts a real problem, and a real problem can live inside a panic.

cards.name: The cult panic: deprogrammers and what they got wrong
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The cult panic: deprogrammers and what they got wrong" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: A panic can distort a real problem, and a real problem can still exist inside a panic. Hold both.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Violence: what predicts it (Waco, Heaven's Gate, Aum Shinrikyo)
cards.q: What does the base rate tell you about violence in new religious movements?
options: It is very rare, so a strange belief alone is a poor warning sign
It is common, so any group with strict rules should be closely watched
It is unknowable, so scholars have stopped comparing the few cases
cards.why: Thousands of groups have existed; only a handful turned violent. Look for combinations, not oddness.

cards.name: Violence: what predicts it (Waco, Heaven's Gate, Aum Shinrikyo)
cards.q: In Wessinger's terms, why are the Branch Davidians an assaulted group?
options: Their mission failed from inside, so they turned on themselves
They planned a war on society, so they struck the first blow
Outsiders attacked them first, and the crisis grew from that
cards.why: The ATF raid opened the crisis. Fragile groups like Jonestown turn violent from within.

cards.name: Violence: what predicts it (Waco, Heaven's Gate, Aum Shinrikyo)
cards.q: What did the 1996 Montana Freemen standoff show?
options: Patient negotiation and an open way out can end a standoff without deaths
Armed groups always surrender as soon as the first deadline is announced
Standoffs end peacefully only when the group has no weapons at all
cards.why: Eighty-one days, applied lessons from Waco, and no deaths. A crisis is not a destiny.

cards.name: Violence: what predicts it (Waco, Heaven's Gate, Aum Shinrikyo)
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Violence: what predicts it (Waco, Heaven's Gate, Aum Shinrikyo)" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The warning sign is not a weird belief. It is a closed system under pressure with no dignified way out.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Leaving and after: exit costs and rebuilding a self
cards.q: Why do many members stay long after their first doubts?
options: Groups lock their doors, so walking out is physically impossible
Leaving would cost friends, home, savings and meaning all at once
Doubts never appear inside, because the group has removed them
cards.why: Exit costs, not certainty, keep most people inside. Doubt is common; a safe place to share it is rare.

cards.name: Leaving and after: exit costs and rebuilding a self
cards.q: What does floating describe?
options: A planned trial period before a member joins for good
A state of calm detachment that leaders train recruits in
A sudden slide back into group thinking after leaving
cards.why: Former members describe triggers, a phrase, a song, that pull the old frame back for a moment.

cards.name: Leaving and after: exit costs and rebuilding a self
cards.q: What is the best first move for a family member of someone inside?
options: Win the argument about doctrine, so that they have to see the truth
Keep in touch, ask curious questions and have practical help ready
Cut contact until they leave, so the group stops feeling worth it
cards.why: People leave towards someone. Debate and ultimatums tend to confirm the group's story about outsiders.

cards.name: Leaving and after: exit costs and rebuilding a self
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Leaving and after: exit costs and rebuilding a self" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Leaving is not one event. It is rebuilding a life with more than one source of reality.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Born inside: second-generation members
cards.q: What makes leaving harder for someone born inside a group?
options: There is no earlier self or outside life to return to
Groups usually let born-in members go without any shunning
They chose the group as adults, so leaving feels like failure
cards.why: No baseline, no outside records, and often the loss of parents and siblings.

cards.name: Born inside: second-generation members
cards.q: What is a total institution in Goffman's sense?
options: Any group with a written doctrine and a charismatic founder
A place where all of life runs under one authority and schedule
A company large enough to employ a whole town at one time
cards.why: Prisons, hospitals, ships, boarding schools and some groups qualify. The shape, not the belief, defines it.

cards.name: Born inside: second-generation members
cards.q: What do second-generation members often do to a movement over time?
options: Push it to change, split or soften as they grow up and compare notes
Leave it untouched, because children rarely question their parents
Make it stricter, because they defend the rules more than converts do
cards.why: Born-in members who leave and speak out have pushed several groups to reform, split or soften.

cards.name: Born inside: second-generation members
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Born inside: second-generation members" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: A convert returns to a self. Someone born inside has to build one, often while losing their family.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Cultish: online groups, wellness, MLMs and startups
cards.q: What did the FTC's 2024 review of 70 MLM income disclosures find?
options: Most participants earned a full-time wage within their first year
Income figures were clear, complete and included all expenses
Most participants received $1,000 or less a year, before expenses
cards.why: Many received nothing. The statements tended to hide the low earners and ignore costs.

cards.name: Cultish: online groups, wellness, MLMs and startups
cards.q: What is the best test for whether a group is cultish in a harmful way?
options: Whether people can disagree, leave and see the money without cost
Whether the group has a logo, a slogan and a charismatic founder
Whether members are very enthusiastic and talk about it constantly
cards.why: Intensity and branding are everywhere. Control over exit, money and dissent is the line.

cards.name: Cultish: online groups, wellness, MLMs and startups
cards.q: What does conspirituality describe?
options: A scholarly method for studying secret religious groups
A blend of conspiracy theory and New Age spirituality
A rule that bans spiritual leaders from running for office
cards.why: Ward and Voas named it in 2011. QAnon travelled through these spaces.

cards.name: Cultish: online groups, wellness, MLMs and startups
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Cultish: online groups, wellness, MLMs and startups" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Intensity is not the test. Ask whether people can disagree, leave and follow the money without paying for it.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: On screen: The Master, Midsommar, The Wicker Man, Martha Marcy May Marlene
cards.q: Which mechanism is the engine of Martha Marcy May Marlene?
options: The siege: the police surround the farm and the group fights back
The recruitment: most of the film shows her first week inside
The after: the group keeps living in her once she has escaped
cards.why: She escapes at the start. The film is about floating, memory and the gifts that made the abuse possible.

cards.name: On screen: The Master, Midsommar, The Wicker Man, Martha Marcy May Marlene
cards.q: What does Midsommar's shared-wailing scene show in Durkheim's terms?
options: Proof that the commune is simply evil and gives her nothing real
Collective emotion giving Dani the belonging nobody else offered
A hidden technique that erases Dani's memory of her own family
cards.why: The group feels her grief with her. The gift is real, which is why the horror works.

cards.name: On screen: The Master, Midsommar, The Wicker Man, Martha Marcy May Marlene
cards.q: What is the writer's rule distilled from this stop?
options: Every scene gives her something she needs or raises the cost of leaving
Every scene explains the doctrine so the audience can judge its logic
Every scene shows the leader hypnotising someone in a new and scary way
cards.why: Gift and price drive the story. Scenes that do neither can go.

cards.name: On screen: The Master, Midsommar, The Wicker Man, Martha Marcy May Marlene
cards.q: Drill "Read a cult film like a researcher": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Name the need: what is missing in the character's life in the first ten minutes? 2) Find the gift: what does the group give that nobody else does? 3) Mark the first small yes, and the first moment saying no would cost something. 4) Spot one of Lifton's eight (stop 1.3) on screen: milieu control, loaded language, confession, and so on. 5) Find the boundary: who is outside, and what is said about them? 6) Decide which myth the film believes: robot, free shopper, or bounded choice (stop 3.3). Usual mistake: Judging the characters as stupid. If you would not have said yes in her place, the film failed, or you have not looked closely enough at the need.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: On screen: The Master, Midsommar, The Wicker Man, Martha Marcy May Marlene
cards.q: Page closed: explain "On screen: The Master, Midsommar, The Wicker Man, Martha Marcy May Marlene" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Make the belonging beautiful enough that the audience feels the loss, then show the price of keeping it.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Anatomy of a con: Maurer's big con, step by step
cards.q: In Maurer's big con, which role makes the first friendly approach?
options: The fixer, who bribes officials after the touch
The inside man, who controls the opportunity
The roper, who wins trust and steers the mark onward
cards.why: The roper approaches and vouches. The inside man plays the expert. Trust is passed between roles.

cards.name: Anatomy of a con: Maurer's big con, step by step
cards.q: What makes a big con "big" rather than short?
options: A crew, a staged world, props and time
A victim with more education than usual
A louder promise of bigger riches
cards.why: A short con is one quick interaction. A big con is a production with roles and a set.

cards.name: Anatomy of a con: Maurer's big con, step by step
cards.q: Following Mercier, what is the best defence against a con?
options: Assuming that intelligent people rarely need checks
Treating every stranger you meet as dishonest
Independent checking and a pause, even when you feel clever
cards.why: People are vigilant by default. Cons make checking feel costly, so build checks that run anyway.

cards.name: Anatomy of a con: Maurer's big con, step by step
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Anatomy of a con: Maurer's big con, step by step" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The mark is not stupid. The room has been designed so that checking feels like betrayal.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig
cards.q: Why did the Eiffel Tower story feel believable to the scrap dealers?
options: The French government had announced a real public auction
The tower's costly upkeep and future were already publicly debated
Gustave Eiffel personally wrote to the dealers in 1925
cards.why: Borrowed truth. The lie grew out of a real argument, so it felt like inside news.

cards.name: The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig
cards.q: What did the "bribe" do for the con?
options: Made the official feel real, and made reporting it shameful
Covered Lustig's hotel bill at the Hotel de Crillon
Proved to the police that the sale had been legal
cards.why: It worked as the convincer and the fix at once: real-seeming corruption, then a silent victim.

cards.name: The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig
cards.q: How accurate is the headline that Lustig "sold it twice"?
options: False: Lustig never went to Paris at all
Fully accurate: two buyers paid in full for the tower
Partly: one sale succeeded and a later attempt failed
cards.why: The tower's own history records one completed sale and a failed second attempt.

cards.name: The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The bribe is not extra plot. It is the mark's exit from embarrassment, and the con man's insurance.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Why smart people fall for cons, and why we are less gullible than films think
cards.q: In the FINRA interviews, which intelligence belief raised the risk of losing money?
options: That you are probably smarter than the person calling you
That not knowing an answer is shameful and lowers your status
That asking questions is how intelligent people learn
cards.why: The need to look smart stops people asking questions. Believing that questions are learning protected them.

cards.name: Why smart people fall for cons, and why we are less gullible than films think
cards.q: What did the AARP survey find about people who lost money to scams?
options: They had far less formal education than non-victims
They had about twice as many stressful life events as non-victims
They were almost always under 30 and new to money
cards.why: Strain narrows attention. Victims reported 4.0 stressful events versus 1.9 for non-victims.

cards.name: Why smart people fall for cons, and why we are less gullible than films think
cards.q: Why can expertise make someone a better target?
options: Confidence in one area spreads to areas you have not checked
Con artists are not allowed to approach professionals
Experts are legally barred from asking for second opinions
cards.why: Knowing the code is not knowing the company. The private exception switches off your own checks.

cards.name: Why smart people fall for cons, and why we are less gullible than films think
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Why smart people fall for cons, and why we are less gullible than films think" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Intelligence does not cancel emotion. It gives emotion a better vocabulary.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The Sting: making the audience the mark
cards.q: How did David Maurer's lawsuit over The Sting end?
options: A jury found the film guilty of plagiarism
The court dismissed it and ordered Maurer to pay costs
It was settled out of court in 1976
cards.why: Maurer sued in 1974 and the case settled in 1976. A settlement is not a finding of plagiarism.

cards.name: The Sting: making the audience the mark
cards.q: What do The Sting's chapter cards do to the audience?
options: Make viewers feel like insiders, so they stop looking for a hidden plan
Reveal the final twist early so viewers can enjoy the craft
Replace the need for any visual clues in the story
cards.why: A map that is true but incomplete works like a roper: it earns trust and lowers your guard.

cards.name: The Sting: making the audience the mark
cards.q: What separates a fair twist from a cheat?
options: A new piece of evidence is introduced after the reveal
The audience is never shown any of the key facts
The facts were shown earlier; only their meaning was hidden
cards.why: Seed the fact, let the audience misread it, then reclassify. A late new fact is a cheat.

cards.name: The Sting: making the audience the mark
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The Sting: making the audience the mark" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: A twist is fair when the audience was given the truth but not the confidence to read it.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Slippin' Jimmy to Saul Goodman
cards.q: Why does Chuck secretly block Jimmy from the Sandpiper case?
options: He thinks the overbilling case has no legal merit
He believes Slippin' Jimmy can never change
He wants Kim Wexler to lead the case instead
cards.why: "Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree is like a chimp with a machine gun." Chuck uses deceit to stop a man he calls deceitful.

cards.name: Slippin' Jimmy to Saul Goodman
cards.q: Which best describes Jimmy's want versus his need?
options: Want: respect as a lawyer. Need: to stop performing to win every room
Want: to quit law. Need: to earn far more money
Want: to be left alone. Need: to become famous
cards.why: Every clever shortcut gets him the want for a day and moves him further from the need.

cards.name: Slippin' Jimmy to Saul Goodman
cards.q: What happens in the finale, Saul Gone?
options: He wins the case and returns to practise law in Albuquerque
He escapes to Omaha and is never caught
He rejects a deal of about seven years, confesses, and gets 86
cards.why: The last performance is the truth. "The name's McGill." It costs him everything a con usually wins.

cards.name: Slippin' Jimmy to Saul Goodman
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Slippin' Jimmy to Saul Goodman" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The con becomes a tragedy when it works for the wrong reason.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Twists that play fair: Nine Queens, House of Games, The Grifters
cards.q: In the fair-twist test, what does a cheat twist depend on?
options: A reveal that changes a relationship between characters
A fact never shown, or the film lying to the viewer directly
A frame that the audience badly wants to believe
cards.why: Fair twists show the facts and hide the connection. Cheats hide the facts or lie outright.

cards.name: Twists that play fair: Nine Queens, House of Games, The Grifters
cards.q: What frame does House of Games use to disarm its audience?
options: Two partners working together against a rich collector
An expert studying con men from what seems a safe distance
A mother and son trying to reconcile after years apart
cards.why: The tutorial is the con. Each true lesson about cons is also a convincer aimed at her.

cards.name: Twists that play fair: Nine Queens, House of Games, The Grifters
cards.q: Why is a twist that changes a relationship stronger than a plot trick?
options: It turns the surprise into an emotional cost the audience feels
It removes the need to seed any facts beforehand
It guarantees that nobody can guess the ending
cards.why: Surprise fades on rewatch. A changed relationship deepens on rewatch.

cards.name: Twists that play fair: Nine Queens, House of Games, The Grifters
cards.q: Drill "Boss fight: the fair-twist audit": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Pick any twist film or episode you know well (not one of the three above). 2) Write its frame in one sentence: what the audience believes it is watching. 3) List every fact the twist depends on and where each was shown. Mark any that were never shown. 4) Name the relationship the twist changes. If none, note it. 5) Score it out of 5 on the checklist and write one fix that would make it fairer. Usual mistake: Confusing surprise with quality. A twist you could never have guessed, even on a rewatch, usually means a fact was withheld, not that the film was clever.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Twists that play fair: Nine Queens, House of Games, The Grifters
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Twists that play fair: Nine Queens, House of Games, The Grifters" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The best con films are better on the rewatch, because the second time you get to be the crew.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Ripley: the identity con as character
cards.q: What makes Ripley an identity con rather than a disguise?
options: The con only needs to fool one person for one evening
Tom wears a mask and fake beard in every scene
The false self must be maintained for months against everyone
cards.why: A disguise lasts a scene. An identity is a job: signatures, clothes, letters, timing.

cards.name: Ripley: the identity con as character
cards.q: How does Highsmith's 1955 novel end for Tom?
options: He gets away with it and stays free in later books
He is arrested on the last page by the Italian police
He confesses to Dickie's father and returns the money
cards.why: A provocation in 1955. Purple Noon (1960) chose to catch him instead.

cards.name: Ripley: the identity con as character
cards.q: Why do audiences root for Tom despite his crimes?
options: Every version makes him a hero who saves other people
They share his knowledge and danger, so his near misses feel like theirs
The stories hide that he has committed any crime at all
cards.why: Alignment. Competence, fear and an outsider's resentment make us his accomplice.

cards.name: Ripley: the identity con as character
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Ripley: the identity con as character" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: An alias is a promise that has to be paid in daily labour.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Real impostors: Clark Rockefeller, Anna Delvey and the Abagnale problem
cards.q: What finally exposed all three impostors in this stop?
options: A single brilliant detective who studied their body language
Each of them confessed voluntarily to a journalist
Ordinary records: custody papers, bank statements, prison files
cards.why: Each sold a social shortcut that made checking feel rude. Paperwork broke them.

cards.name: Real impostors: Clark Rockefeller, Anna Delvey and the Abagnale problem
cards.q: What did Alan Logan's 2020 research claim about Frank Abagnale?
options: Records show him in custody for much of the period he described
He never existed and the memoir was written by Spielberg
Every claim in Catch Me If You Can was confirmed by Pan Am
cards.why: A records-based challenge, not a court ruling. The famous story is contested and weakly supported.

cards.name: Real impostors: Clark Rockefeller, Anna Delvey and the Abagnale problem
cards.q: What was Christian Gerhartsreiter convicted of in 2013?
options: Stealing more than $200,000 from New York hotels
Posing as a Rockefeller, which is a federal crime
The 1985 murder of John Sohus, his landlady's son
cards.why: A jury in Los Angeles convicted him; he was sentenced to 27 years to life. Linda Sohus was never found.

cards.name: Real impostors: Clark Rockefeller, Anna Delvey and the Abagnale problem
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Real impostors: Clark Rockefeller, Anna Delvey and the Abagnale problem" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Impostors are rarely caught by geniuses. They are caught by someone who finally reads the paperwork.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: The gentleman thief: Lupin
cards.q: What disguise gets Assane into the Louvre in the first episode?
options: A forged invitation to a private gala
A job on the museum's cleaning crew
A police uniform borrowed from a friend
cards.why: He hides behind other people's assumptions. The wealthy never look at a cleaner's face.

cards.name: The gentleman thief: Lupin
cards.q: Which ingredient lets an audience enjoy a gentleman thief's crimes?
options: A code: he steals from the powerful and protects the weak
Violence: he is the most dangerous man in every room
Realism: every heist could be copied step by step
cards.why: Disguise, theatre, a code and invisibility. The code makes the crime feel just.

cards.name: The gentleman thief: Lupin
cards.q: What does "adaptation by one variable" mean in Lupin's case?
options: Copy Leblanc's stories scene by scene into modern dress
Keep the charm and disguise, change who the hero is
Replace the thief with a detective who hunts him
cards.why: Assane is an immigrant's son. One change makes a 1905 hero speak about 2021.

cards.name: The gentleman thief: Lupin
cards.q: Page closed: explain "The gentleman thief: Lupin" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The best disguise is the role society has already decided not to look at.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Ocean's and the crew film
cards.q: What is the genre's "plan behind the plan"?
options: The backup plan the crew writes down before the job
The police plan to catch the crew in the sequel
A hidden layer of the scheme revealed at the end
cards.why: The film explains a plan, then reveals another layer. The Sting's trick, made into a genre.

cards.name: Ocean's and the crew film
cards.q: Why does the recruitment section work so well?
options: Each specialist is shown doing the one thing they do best
It explains every step of the heist in technical detail
It gives every crew member a long backstory monologue
cards.why: One trait, one skill, one joke. Competence on screen is its own suspense.

cards.name: Ocean's and the crew film
cards.q: What gives the money in Ocean's Eleven a personal stake?
options: The crew plans to donate the money to charity
Danny's ex-wife Tess is with the casino owner
Danny owes the money to the boxing promoter
cards.why: A heist with a relationship at stake ends when a person decides, not when a vault opens.

cards.name: Ocean's and the crew film
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Ocean's and the crew film" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The heist is the plot. Whether the crew can trust each other is the story.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Real heists: Antwerp, Hatton Garden, the Louvre 2025
cards.q: What led police to the Antwerp crew?
options: An insider who confessed the morning after the job
A fingerprint left on the vault door
A bag of rubbish dumped near the E19 motorway
cards.why: Documents and a half-eaten sandwich in the rubbish linked the crew. The getaway was the weak point.

cards.name: Real heists: Antwerp, Hatton Garden, the Louvre 2025
cards.q: Where does the pattern across the three cases put the failure?
options: In the vault, which none of the crews could fully open
In the everyday aftermath: cars, rubbish, talk, a dropped item
In the planning, which all three crews rushed
cards.why: Skill went into the target. The mundane parts nobody rehearsed undid them.

cards.name: Real heists: Antwerp, Hatton Garden, the Louvre 2025
cards.q: A year after the Louvre theft, what was the state of the case?
options: Arrests made and suspects jailed, but the jewels still missing
All eight items recovered and returned to the gallery
No arrests and no suspects identified
cards.why: France24 reported at least seven arrests and four jailed suspects, but no recovered jewels.

cards.name: Real heists: Antwerp, Hatton Garden, the Louvre 2025
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Real heists: Antwerp, Hatton Garden, the Louvre 2025" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The vault is the hard part on paper. The everyday part is where real crews get caught.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Social engineering: the con inside the heist
cards.q: How was MGM Resorts reportedly breached in September 2023?
options: A flaw in the casino slot machine software
A stolen laptop left in a hotel room
A call to its IT help desk by someone posing as an employee
cards.why: A plausible voice and a process that rewarded speed. No exotic code needed.

cards.name: Social engineering: the con inside the heist
cards.q: What is the strongest defence against a convincing urgent call?
options: Call back on a number you already hold
Ask the caller to confirm their name twice
Trust your gut about how they sound
cards.why: A call-back removes the judgement call. Voices and names can be faked; your own number cannot.

cards.name: Social engineering: the con inside the heist
cards.q: What share of 2024 breaches did Verizon link to a non-malicious human element?
cards.why: Verizon's 2024 report put it at 68%. People, not code, are the usual entry point.

cards.name: Social engineering: the con inside the heist
cards.q: Drill "Boss fight: the masks audit": what are the steps, and the usual mistake?
cards.answer: 1) Pick one con or heist from File 5 (Ripley, Delvey, Lupin, Ocean's, Antwerp, Hatton Garden, the Louvre or MGM). 2) Name the mask: the role the con artist or crew played, and who it was played for. 3) Name the moment a single person could have broken it with one check. 4) Now turn it on yourself: list three accounts or payments in your own work that a convincing voice could reach. 5) For each, write the check you will use from now on: call-back, named approver or a written rule. Usual mistake: Thinking you are too sharp to fall for it. The cases in this file beat banks, casinos and a museum. The defence is a habit you use when you feel sure, not a feeling of being clever.
cards.label: Drill

cards.name: Social engineering: the con inside the heist
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Social engineering: the con inside the heist" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The attacker needs one person to skip one check. Defence is a habit, not a gadget.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Ponzi and affinity fraud: from Charles Ponzi to Madoff
cards.q: What keeps a Ponzi scheme alive?
options: Profits from a real but secret trading strategy
New investors’ money paying earlier investors
Government insurance on the deposits
cards.why: There is no business inside the loop. The fuel is the next investor, and it dies when withdrawals beat deposits.

cards.name: Ponzi and affinity fraud: from Charles Ponzi to Madoff
cards.q: What makes affinity fraud so effective?
options: It always uses complex financial products
It only targets people with no investing experience
It borrows the trust members of a group already have in each other
cards.why: The trust is real but pointed at the wrong thing. People trust the introducer and skip the checks.

cards.name: Ponzi and affinity fraud: from Charles Ponzi to Madoff
cards.q: What did Madoff tell two senior employees before the SEC charged him?
options: That it was “basically, a giant Ponzi scheme”
That a rogue trader had lost the money
That hackers had emptied the accounts
cards.why: The SEC’s December 2008 release quotes him. He also said it was “all just one big lie”.

cards.name: Ponzi and affinity fraud: from Charles Ponzi to Madoff
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Ponzi and affinity fraud: from Charles Ponzi to Madoff" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: The first payment proves only that money moved, not why it moved.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Ponzi, pyramid or MLM: telling them apart
cards.q: What is the FTC’s key test for whether an MLM pays people legitimately?
options: Whether rewards come from real retail sales, not recruiting
Whether the company sells a real product
Whether the founder is personally wealthy
cards.why: A product can be a cover. What matters is who the real customer is and where the money comes from.

cards.name: Ponzi, pyramid or MLM: telling them apart
cards.q: If each member must recruit six people, roughly how many levels until a pyramid needs more people than exist?
options: A hundred levels
Thirteen levels
Thirty levels
cards.why: Six to the thirteenth power is about 13 billion, more than everyone alive. The base always loses.

cards.name: Ponzi, pyramid or MLM: telling them apart
cards.q: What did the AARP Foundation’s 2018 survey find about MLM participants?
options: About half earned over $10,000 a year
Most made a steady part-time income
Nearly half lost money and about a quarter broke even
cards.why: Only about a quarter made a profit, and more than half of those made under $5,000.

cards.name: Ponzi, pyramid or MLM: telling them apart
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Ponzi, pyramid or MLM: telling them apart" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Follow the money to the real customer. If the customer is the next recruit, it is a pyramid.
cards.label: Say it in the room

cards.name: Theranos: the story that outran the science
cards.q: What did Carreyrou report about Theranos’s own device by the end of 2014?
options: It had been banned outright by regulators
It handled only a small fraction of the tests sold to consumers
It ran every test but was too slow
cards.why: Most tests ran on machines bought from other makers. The story was far ahead of the science.

cards.name: Theranos: the story that outran the science
cards.q: On which counts was Elizabeth Holmes convicted in January 2022?
options: Four counts of defrauding investors
All counts, including those about patients
Only counts about patients
cards.why: She was acquitted on the patient counts. Balwani was convicted on all twelve counts he faced.

cards.name: Theranos: the story that outran the science
cards.q: Why did a board of famous statesmen reassure investors?
options: Their names felt like proof, though none of them tested the science
They had personally run the blood tests
They guaranteed the investors’ money
cards.why: Borrowed authority is a convincer. It feels like evidence without being evidence.

cards.name: Theranos: the story that outran the science
cards.q: Page closed: explain "Theranos: the story that outran the science" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: A demo that worked once is not a product. Show the evidence, not the vision.

cards.name: FTX and Wirecard: when nobody checks
cards.q: What did FTX’s new chief executive say he had never seen in his career?
options: A founder who cooperated so fully
A crypto exchange with so many customers
Such a complete failure of corporate controls
cards.why: Ray, who had handled Enron, also found no trustworthy financial information and payments approved by emoji.

cards.name: FTX and Wirecard: when nobody checks
cards.q: How did Germany’s regulator respond to critical reports about Wirecard in 2019?
options: It banned short selling and filed a complaint against FT reporters
It suspended the chief executive pending an inquiry
It ordered an immediate audit of the Asian accounts
cards.why: BaFin protected the company and pursued the journalists. The journalists were right.

cards.name: FTX and Wirecard: when nobody checks
cards.q: What is the main lesson FTX and Wirecard share?
options: Each check assumed another check was working
Crypto is always riskier than payments
Short sellers cause company collapses
cards.why: Auditors, boards, regulators and investors each relied on the others. The outsiders who checked were attacked.

cards.name: FTX and Wirecard: when nobody checks
cards.q: Page closed: explain "FTX and Wirecard: when nobody checks" in two or three lines, as you would to a client.
cards.answer: Every check thought another check was working. Be the one who actually looks.
